name: The Early Warning System
title: The Early Warning System
answer: An early warning system tracks indicators that predict whether a student is falling off track, such as attendance, behavior incidents, and course performance, reviewed weekly or monthly. It matters because a flag should lead to a person reaching out, and published indicators let families and staff understand why a student was flagged. The system is a reason to ask, not an answer.

crumbs.name: Assessment, Data, and the Early Warning System

sections.body: An early warning system is a routine way to watch signs that a student may be losing ground. It brings together attendance, behavior incidents, and course performance so that staff can review them on a weekly or monthly cycle. The problem it solves is that without a shared signal, concerns can stay scattered or arrive too late for a helpful conversation. The same principle from attendance applies to every indicator: a flag should lead to a person who reaches out. Clear, published indicators are safer than hidden scores because everyone can see why a student was flagged.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a district might publish that students are flagged when they miss more than a certain number of days, receive a set number of behavior referrals, or fail a core course. Staff then review those indicators weekly or monthly, and when a student is flagged, the conversation starts from shared understanding. The text does not give separate grade band examples, so the same structure applies across a school: attendance, behavior incidents, and course performance are watched, and a person reaches out. Families and staff can see the rules, which helps them understand the flag together. The flag itself is not the intervention; it is the prompt for a human conversation.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book reports research findings rather than a single evidence label. Soland et al., 2020, found that machine learning can sharpen predictions and even help create clear rules, but it takes expertise to use well, and systems whose reasoning is hidden invite users to interpret results through their existing biases. Hlosta et al., 2022, interviewed students whose risk predictions were wrong and found that the errors came from sudden life events, such as family changes, health problems, or technology trouble. Bertolini et al., 2022, adds that variability in predictions adds to the uncertainty. The text's overall finding is that a flag is a reason to ask, not an answer.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are that predictions miss what data cannot see, and hidden scores can lead people to fill in reasons with stereotypes. A counselor who sees a flag with no explanation may fill in the reason with a stereotype, so clear, published indicators are safer. Machine learning can improve predictions, but it takes expertise to use well, and the reasoning must not be hidden. The decisions that stay with a person are the outreach and the conversation, because attendance flags and every other indicator should lead to a person who reaches out. A flag is a reason to ask, not an answer, and sudden life events such as family changes, health problems, or technology trouble may explain an error.
